passage: At her cousin's engagement in Bhilwara, Vandana had tried to join the older girls' conversation and said, too loudly, "Oh, I thought she was your mother!" about a woman who turned out to be the girl's elder sister. There was a pause, then laughter, then the talk moved on. But for Vandana, it didn't. Walking home past the stepwell, she replayed it. Lying on the roof that night, she replayed it again, each time a little worse. On Tuesday, grinding masala with her mother, she thought of a better line she could have said. By Wednesday she was sure the whole mohalla knew. When Madhuri asked why she'd gone so quiet, Vandana said, "I'm just trying to figure out how to fix it." But nothing she came up with fixed anything. It only stung more.

qa.q: What did Vandana say too loudly at the engagement?
qa.a: "Oh, I thought she was your mother!"

qa.q: Why does Vandana feel she is "trying to figure out how to fix it"?
qa.a: Replaying the moment feels like working on the problem, so it seems useful, even though each replay only makes the embarrassment sharper.

qa.q: What could help Vandana break the replay?
qa.a: Noticing that the talk moved on within seconds, and turning her attention to something absorbing when the memory returns, rather than rehearsing new lines.

qa.q: How might the older girls remember the moment?
qa.a: They probably laughed briefly and forgot it, unlike Vandana, who imagines the whole mohalla still talking about it.

passage: At Felix's sixteenth birthday party in Vancouver, Mei tried to make a joke about his new haircut. It came out wrong: "Did you lose a bet?" Felix laughed, sort of. Someone said, "Ouch." That was Saturday. By Wednesday, Mei had replayed it maybe a hundred times: in the shower, on the bus, in the middle of chemistry. She imagined Felix telling everyone. She imagined them all remembering it every time they saw her. She drafted three apology texts and deleted them all. Each replay felt like working out the problem, but each one made her face burn hotter. On Thursday Felix sat next to her at lunch and chatted about basketball as if nothing had happened. Mei barely heard a word.

qa.q: What joke did Mei make about Felix's haircut?
qa.a: "Did you lose a bet?"

qa.q: Why did Mei keep replaying the joke?
qa.a: Each replay felt like solving the problem, as if thinking it through enough would undo it, but it only made her more embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Mei try on Thursday instead of barely listening?

qa.q: How does Felix seem to see the moment by Thursday?
qa.a: Felix seems to have moved on completely, chatting about basketball as if nothing happened, unlike Mei.

passage: At the school's Class 10 farewell, Chandrika had been asked to say a few words on stage, and in her nervousness she called their class teacher "Mummy" into the microphone. The hall exploded with laughter. The teacher laughed too, kindly. Three days later, Chandrika still hadn't stopped replaying it. In the library she stared at the same page. In the corridor, every laugh seemed to be about her. She went over what she should have said, sentence by sentence, as if she could solve it. On Monday the school counsellor, Mr Amandeep, found her alone on the steps. "You look like you're carrying something heavy," he said. Chandrika said, "I'm just thinking it through." "How many times have you thought it through?" She didn't know. Too many.

qa.a: "Mummy."

qa.q: Why does Chandrika say she is "just thinking it through"?
qa.a: Going over it sentence by sentence feels like solving the problem, so it seems sensible, even as it keeps the embarrassment fresh.

Dear Reena chechi,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Okay, here it is.
At Alan's birthday party on Saturday, everyone was praising the cake and I said, loudly, "Did you get it from the bakery? It tastes bought." His mum had made it herself. She was standing right behind me.

Is this normal? Did you ever do this?
Joseph

passage: Shankar, you're still thinking about what you said at the party, na? Let me tell you something. When I was a girl of fifteen, in Thrissur, at my friend Latha's house for Onam, I told her mother that her payasam was "too sweet, like my aunty's." I meant it as a joke. Everyone went quiet. Latha's mother just smiled. I went home and couldn't sleep. For a whole week I replayed it, again and again. I imagined Latha's family talking about me at dinner. I practised apologies in the mirror. I even avoided walking past her house. Each time I replayed it, I felt smaller. Finally, I went to Latha and said sorry. She laughed. "Gopika, Amma thought it was funny. She told everyone she makes it too sweet on purpose." A whole week of pain, for nothing.

passage: It was exam week, and Jasleen had a chemistry paper on Monday. But all Sunday, she couldn't focus. At her cousin's engagement on Saturday, she'd called her cousin's fiancé by the wrong name in front of his whole family. Raghav, her other cousin, had said, "It's okay, happens," but she had seen someone smirk. Now she sat with the textbook open and replayed it. She remembered the smirk. She imagined the family laughing about it at dinner. She thought of messages she could send to apologise, and deleted them. She told herself she was just working out how to fix it. But after three hours she'd read one page, and her face still burned. At night Raghav texted, "Stop thinking about it. Nobody cares." She read it twice. It didn't help. She kept replaying it until two.

I'm Mridul, and this happened over the summer holidays.

At Parveen's farewell party I tried to make a speech. I said, "We'll all miss you, even though you never share your chips." It was meant to be funny. Nobody laughed. Parveen smiled, kind of.

For the next five days I replayed it. Brushing my teeth, on my cycle, during cricket. Each time I added something worse: maybe Parveen cried later, maybe everyone had messaged about it. I kept thinking I was working it out, like a sum. I wasn't. I was just pressing the bruise.

On the sixth day Parveen sent me a voice note from the new city: "Mridul, send the photos from the party!" Totally normal voice.

I felt stupid and relieved at once. Now when a line starts looping, I ask myself: is this solving anything, or just pressing the bruise?

qa.a: Mridul replayed it for the next five days.

qa.a: Mridul asks whether the loop is solving anything or just pressing the bruise; it helps Mridul notice when thinking has turned into hurting.

School counsellor's note — Seema
Lokesh, Class 9, came in on Thursday. At a classmate's birthday party on Saturday, when the girl's mother asked him if he wanted more cake, he said, "No thanks, Aunty, I'm full of your daughter." He meant to say "full, thanks to your daughter's cake." A few people laughed.
He has replayed it, he says, "maybe a hundred times." He cannot sleep. He thinks everyone in class is still talking about it, though when I asked whether anyone had mentioned it since Monday, he admitted nobody had.
He said, "I keep going over it to figure out how to fix it." But each replay makes him feel worse.
We practised noticing when the replay starts and saying to himself, "That's the party tape again," then doing something else. I will see him again next week.

qa.q: Why does Lokesh keep replaying the moment?
